'''Mexico City Texcoco Airport''' was a planned airport in [[Mexico City]] that was meant to become Mexico's New International Airport (Spanish: '''''Nuevo Aeropuerto Internacional de México'''''—'''NAICM''' or '''NAIM'''). The project was announced in September 2014 but was canceled in late 2018 after a referendum was held stating that the new airport should be built at a different location due to how close it was to housing, rising cost and a geographical issue with the site.

Texcoco Airport was first announced by [[President of Mexico|President]] [[Enrique Peña Nieto]] in his State of the Union Address on 2 September 2014. It was billed as Mexico's largest public infrastructure work in a century, and was set to replace Mexico City's current [[Mexico City International Airport|Benito Juárez International Airport]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aicm.com.mx/estadisticas|title=Estadísticas del AICM (in Spanish)|website=Aeropuerto Internacional de la Ciudad de México|date=6 March 2014 }}</ref>

In October 2018, while construction was already taking place, a non-binding referendum was organized by then President-elect [[Andrés Manuel López Obrador]], in which almost 70 percent of the 1.067 million voters rejected the planned airport, choosing instead to build a new airport on the grounds of [[Mexico City Santa Lucía Airport|Santa Lucía Air Force Base]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Redacción|url=https://www.bbc.com/mundo/noticias-america-latina-46015692|title=Mayoría de votantes en consulta sobre nuevo aeropuerto en México rechaza su construcción|date=2018-10-29|publisher=BBC News Mundo|access-date=February 14, 2020|language=es}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dezeen.com/2018/10/30/foster-partners-fernando-romero-mexico-city-airport-nixed-public-vote/|title=Foster's $13 billion Mexico City airport nixed after public vote|date=30 October 2018|website=Dezeen}}</ref> [[Felipe Ángeles International Airport]] opened in March 2022.

Construction continued for several weeks, but was suspended on 27 December 2018 after López Obrador took office.<ref>{{cite web|title=Obra del NAIM sigue mientras gobierno negocia con acreedores|url=https://www.animalpolitico.com/2018/12/construccion-naim-continua-gacm/|date=3 December 2018|website=Animal Político}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.eluniversal.com.mx/cartera/construccion-de-nuevo-aeropuerto-en-texcoco-esta-oficialmente-suspendida-jimenez-espriu/|title=Construcción de nuevo aeropuerto en Texcoco está oficialmente suspendida: Jiménez Espriú|author=Alberto Morales|date=3 January 2019|work=El Universal|lang=es}}</ref> In 2020, the government of Mexico announced that they would convert the {{convert|12,000|hectare|sqmi|adj=on}} space where the airport was being built into the [[Lake Texcoco Ecological Park]], which will be a public space and an area of [[ecological restoration]].

==Location==
Texcoco Airport was to be constructed on a {{convert|44|km2|adj=on}} site in the ''Zona Federal del Lago de Texcoco'', in part of the dry bed of [[Lake Texcoco]].<ref name=":0" /> The site was only {{convert|3|mi|0|order=flip}} away from the existing [[Mexico City International Airport|Benito Juárez Airport]], making the simultaneous operation of the airports impossible. It was therefore planned that all operations and traffic from Benito Juárez would be transferred to NAIM upon the airport reaching operational status.

== Costs and financing ==
The total cost for construction and initial operation of NAIM was estimated at up to US$13.3 billion, of which approximately 60% was to be contributed by the Mexican government through public funds, and approximately 40% was expected to be funded through a combination of bank loans and the offering of debt securities.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=http://www.aeropuerto.gob.mx/doc/inversionistas/GACM-OM-ING-VP.pdf|title=Bond Offering Memorandum|last=Mexico City Airport Trust|website=GACM}}</ref>

The ''Grupo Aeroportuario de la Ciudad de México'' (GACM), which is fully owned by the Mexican [[Secretariat of Communications and Transportation (Mexico)|Secretariat of Communications and Transportation]] (SCT), was to build and operate the new airport. The GACM created a special purpose trust, the Mexico City Airport Trust, in order to execute the airport's private financing. The trust structured the private contributions as securities drawing from passenger charges at the existing AICM and the future passenger charges of the new airport, without recourse to the Mexican government or the airport sponsors. This collateral structure was designed to ensure that even if the project were to be canceled, the issued bonds would still be honored.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="TWSJ" />

In September 2017, the Mexico City Airport Trust successfully placed US$4 billion in private debt securities for the financing of NAIM. $2 billion were issued in long-term [[Climate bond|green bonds]]. This green bond issuance became the largest in [[Latin America]] at the time and the first green bond from an [[emerging market]] to receive a Green Bond Assessment grade from [[Moody's Investors Service]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Bono verde aportará 4 mil millones de dólares para el Nuevo Aeropuerto Internacional |url=http://www.elfinanciero.com.mx/empresas/bono-verde-aportara-mil-millones-de-dolares-para-el-nuevo-aeropuerto-internacional.html |website=www.elfinanciero.com.mx |date=14 September 2017 |access-date=2 October 2017}}</ref><ref name="TWSJ">{{cite web |title=Mexico Sells $2 Billion in Green Bonds to Help Finance Airport |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/mexico-sells-2-billion-in-green-bonds-to-help-finance-airport-1474650693 |work=The Wall Street Journal |access-date=24 September 2016}}</ref>

==Facilities==
[[File:Proyecto Hidraulico NAICM.jpg|thumb|NAICM and Hydraulic Project]]
[[File:Sitio NAICM 2015.jpg|thumb|NAICM site in 2015]]
The facilities at NAIM were planned to be completed in several stages. By 20 October 2020, the airport was expected to have one main terminal of {{convert|743,000|m2|order=flip}} and three independent runways, which would yield a capacity for 68 million passengers annually. By 2065, the airport was expected to host six runways, an additional main terminal, and two satellite terminals, giving it a capacity for 125 million passengers. This would have made NAIM the second largest airport in the world.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.aeropuerto.gob.mx/doc/pdf/naicm-interiores-vf.pdf|title=Programa Estrategico / Institucional|website=Grupo Aeroportuario de la Ciudad de Mexico (GACM)}}</ref>

The construction plan for the airport was developed by the global engineering and consultancy company [[Arup Group Limited]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.airport-world.com/news/general-news/4122-plans-for-a-new-mexico-city-airport-being-reviewed.html |title=Plans for a new Mexico City Airport being reviewed - Airport World Magazine |publisher=Airport-world.com |date=25 June 2014 |access-date=12 November 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Alper |first=Alexandra |title=New airport plan for Mexico City eyes six runways: sources |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-mexico-airport-idUSKBN0EU1TC20140619 |publisher=Reuters |date=19 June 2014 |access-date=12 November 2015}}</ref> The architectural project was to be designed in collaboration by [[Norman Foster, Baron Foster of Thames Bank|Norman Foster]], who worked on [[Beijing Capital International Airport]] and [[Hong Kong International Airport]], and Mexican architect [[Fernando Romero]], who worked on the [[Soumaya Museum]].

===Terminal design===

The entrance to the terminal was to feature a garden of cacti and symbols of the eagle and snake, part of the national symbol pictured on the country's [[Coat of arms of Mexico|Coat of Arms]] and [[Flag of Mexico|flag]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-09-04 |title=Norman Foster, Romero to build Mexico airport |url=https://apnews.com/general-news-travel-ea1b5c57d4f64fe4818180e3c7bf41bf |access-date=2025-10-27 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

The main terminal was to be constructed in an X shape, which is considered an efficient way to extend the number of gates, and is used in many other airports. The X shape is also thought to be symbolic of the country's name, "México".<ref name=cnn1>{{cite web |url=http://mexico.cnn.com/nacional/2014/09/04/9-puntos-clave-sobre-el-nuevo-aeropuerto-de-la-ciudad-de-mexico |title=9 puntos clave sobre el nuevo aeropuerto de la Ciudad de México - Exportaciones - Nacional - CNNMexico.com |publisher=Mexico.cnn.com |access-date=2015-11-12 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151109102407/http://mexico.cnn.com/nacional/2014/09/04/9-puntos-clave-sobre-el-nuevo-aeropuerto-de-la-ciudad-de-mexico |archive-date=2015-11-09 }}</ref>

According to the architects, the terminal was to be built in the style of [[Mexican architecture]] and was to be much larger than typical terminals, with a maximum internal span in excess of {{convert|170|m|ft}}. The roof was to be made of a lightweight membrane-like material. The whole terminal was to be constructed using pre-fabricated segments.<ref>{{cite web |title=Norman Foster, Romero to build Mexico airport |url=http://readingeagle.com/article/20140903/AP/309039414/1011#sthash.J63U2dWb.dpuf |url-status=dead |publisher=Reading Eagle |date=3 September 2014 |access-date=12 November 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303223110/http://www.readingeagle.com/article/20140903/AP/309039414/1011#sthash.J63U2dWb.dpuf |archive-date=3 March 2016}}</ref><ref name=fosterpress/>

===Sustainability===
The project claimed it was "designed to be the world’s most sustainable airport", and was aiming for a [[LEED|LEED Platinum certification.]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gizmodo.com/mexico-citys-new-mega-airport-will-collect-its-own-ener-1630253952 |title=Mexico City's New Mega-Airport Will Collect Its Own Energy and Water |date=3 September 2014 |publisher=Gizmodo.com |access-date=2015-11-12}}</ref><ref name=fosterpress>{{cite web|url=http://www.fosterandpartners.com/news/archive/2014/09/httpwwwfosterandpartnerscomnewsarchive201409foster-and-partners-to-design-new-international-airport-for-mexico-city/|title=F+P & FR-EE Fernando Romero to collaborate|publisher=Fosterandpartners.com|access-date=12 November 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151115032019/http://www.fosterandpartners.com/news/archive/2014/09/httpwwwfosterandpartnerscomnewsarchive201409foster-and-partners-to-design-new-international-airport-for-mexico-city/|archive-date=15 November 2015}}</ref>

== Antecedents and protests ==
In 2002, President [[Vicente Fox]] announced the construction of a new, larger airport on {{convert|5000|ha|abbr=on}} of land in the municipalities of [[Texcoco, Mexico State|Texcoco]] and [[San Salvador Atenco]] in the same area as the new airport is planned today. When protests held by the [[Community Front in Defense of Land]] - an organization of locals who were to be displaced - were violently repressed,<ref>{{cite news |last=Berehulak |first=Daniel |title=The Women of Atenco |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2016/09/22/world/americas/women-of-atenco.html |access-date=2022-03-24 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=21 September 2016 }}</ref> the new airport was cancelled.<ref>{{cite news |last=Thompson |first=Ginger |title=Mexico Drops Planned Airport After Protests From Peasants |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/08/03/world/mexico-drops-planned-airport-after-protests-from-peasants.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=3 August 2002 |access-date=12 November 2015}}</ref> 

Prior to the 2014 announcement of the construction of the new airport, the government had purchased ''[[ejido]]'' land (agricultural land held in common by local communities), in order to make space for the new airport. Some local groups in [[San Salvador Atenco|Atenco]] and nearby communities claimed that the federal government had acquired the land through deception and strong-arming, and small-scale protests took place after the announcement.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.jornada.unam.mx/ultimas/2014/09/03/con-toma-simbolica-de-maquinaria-atenco-inicia-protestas-contra-el-aeropuerto-6342.html|title=Con "toma" de maquinaria, Atenco inicia protestas contra aeropuerto — La Jornada|language=es|publisher=Jornada.unam.mx|access-date=12 November 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074342/http://www.jornada.unam.mx/ultimas/2014/09/03/con-toma-simbolica-de-maquinaria-atenco-inicia-protestas-contra-el-aeropuerto-6342.html|archive-date=4 March 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eluniversal.com.mx/ciudad-metropoli/2014/reactivan-lucha-en-atenco-contra-aeropuerto-1034993.html |title=DF - Reactivan lucha en Atenco contra aeropuerto |publisher=El Universal |access-date=12 November 2015}}</ref>
The airport plan drew negative reactions across social media with the new movement, #YoPriefieroElLago,<ref>{{Cite news |last=RamÍrez |first=Salvador Ferrer |date=7 October 2018 |title=La campaña #yo prefiero el lago |work=El Universal |url=https://www.eluniversal.com.mx/articulo/salvador-ferrer-ramirez/nacion/la-campana-yo-prefiero-el-lago/ |access-date=11 April 2023}}</ref> in which the distribution of infographics and "fast facts" spread across various platforms. The movement culminated in the creation of a mini-documentary<ref>[https://bombozila.com/es/yo-prefiero-el-lago-mexico/ mini-documentary]</ref> of the same name documenting the airport plan, the land and space it would require, interviews with Atenco community members, and the proliferation of the social media movement.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-10-19 |title=Yo Prefiero el Lago - México |url=https://bombozila.com/es/yo-prefiero-el-lago-mexico/ |access-date=2022-11-16 |website=Bombozila |language=es-ES}}</ref>

'''<big>Post-closure</big>'''

According to the SCT, cancellation of the project left a debt of US$6 billion in bonds and $30 billion in securities, which will be paid off through the [[landing fee]]s at [[Mexico City International Airport|Benito Juárez International Airport]] over a period of 19 years. This debt is in addition to the $56.8 billion paid to the GACM as compensation for the cessation agreement of the fees. None of the money raised through the landing fees at Benito Juárez can be allocated for the construction of the new [[Mexico City Santa Lucía Airport]] or for maintenance of the current airport.<ref>{{cite web |title=A canceled airport will become a financial burden for passengers |url=https://www.eluniversal.com.mx/english/canceled-airport-will-become-financial-burden-passengers |website=El Universal |access-date=13 August 2020 |language=es |date=24 June 2019}}</ref>

In early 2021, the [[Superior Auditor of the Federation]] estimated that cancelling the airport would cost 113 billion pesos.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.yucatan.com.mx/mexico/cancelar-el-aeropuerto-de-la-cdmx-costo-113-millones-de-pesos|title=Cancelar el aeropuerto de la CDMX costó 113 millones de pesos|date=9 May 2021|work=Diario de Yucatán|lang=es}}</ref>

===Alleged fraud===
On 10 July 2020, it was alleged that ''Grupo Gilbert'' had fraudulently won possession of 49,000 tons of steel that had originally been designated for the NAIM.<ref>{{cite web |title=Denuncian corrupción en licitación por venta de acero del NAIM |url=https://www.msn.com/es-mx/dinero/noticias/denuncian-corrupci%c3%b3n-en-licitaci%c3%b3n-por-venta-de-acero-del-naim/ar-BB16ymeF |website=www.msn.com |access-date=10 July 2020}}</ref>

On 12 August 2020, Hugo Bello, leader of the ''Confederacón Libertad de Trabajadores de México'' (Freedom Confederation of Mexican Workers), was arrested for kidnapping and for suspected involvement in embezzlement of money destined for construction of the now-defunct airport.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hugo Bello, detenido ayer, es investigado por desvío millonario en NAIM |url=https://www.eluniversal.com.mx/nacion/hugo-bello-detenido-ayer-es-investigado-por-desvio-millonario-en-naim |website=El Universal |date=13 August 2020 |access-date=13 August 2020 |language=es}}</ref>
